question: What does Part 7 provide regarding recall classification and firm-initiated recalls?
evidence:
[21 CFR 7.3] Definitions.
(a) (a) Agency means the Food and Drug Administration.
(b) (b) Citation or cite means a document and any attachments thereto that provide notice to a person against whom criminal prosecution is contemplated of the opportunity to present views to the agency regarding an alleged violation.
(c) (c) Respondent means a person named in a notice who presents views concerning an alleged violation either in person, by designated representative, or in writing.
(d) (d) Responsible individual includes those in positions of power or authority to detect, prevent, or correct violations of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.
(e) (e) [Reserved]
(f) (f) Product means an article subject to the jurisdiction of the Food and Drug Administration, including any food, drug, and device intended for human or animal use, any cosmetic and biologic intended for human use, any tobacco product intended for human use, and any item subject to a quarantine regulation under part 1240 of this chapter. Product does not include an electronic product that emits radiation and is subject to parts 1003 and 1004 of this chapter.
(g) (g) Recall means a firm's removal or correction of a marketed product that the Food and Drug Administration considers to be in violation of the laws it administers and against which the agency would initiate legal action, e.g., seizure. Recall does not include a market withdrawal or a stock recovery.
(h) (h) Correction means repair, modification, adjustment, relabeling, destruction, or inspection (including patient monitoring) of a product without its physical removal to some other location.
(i) (i) Recalling firm means the firm that initiates a recall or, in the case of a Food and Drug Administration-requested recall, the firm that has primary responsibility for the manufacture and marketing of the product to be recalled.
(j) (j) Market withdrawal means a firm's removal or correction of a distributed product which involves a minor violation that would not be subject to legal action by the Food and Drug Administration or which involves no violation, e.g., normal stock rotation practices, routine equipment adjustments and repairs, etc.
(k) (k) Stock recovery means a firm's removal or correction of a product that has not been marketed or that has not left the direct control of the firm, i.e., the product is located on premises owned by, or under the control of, the firm and no portion of the lot has been released for sale or use.
(l) (l) Recall strategy means a planned specific course of action to be taken in conducting a specific recall, which addresses the depth of recall, need for public warnings, and extent of effectiveness checks for the recall.
(m) (m) Recall classification means the numerical designation, i.e., I, II, or III, assigned by the Food and Drug Administration to a particular product recall to indicate the relative degree of health hazard presented by the product being recalled.
(m)(1) (1) Class I is a situation in which there is a reasonable probability that the use of, or exposure to, a violative product will cause serious adverse health consequences or death.
(m)(2) (2) Class II is a situation in which use of, or exposure to, a violative product may cause temporary or medically reversible adverse health consequences or where the probability of serious adverse health consequences is remote.
(m)(3) (3) Class III is a situation in which use of, or exposure to, a violative product is not likely to cause adverse health consequences.
(n) (n) Consignee means anyone who received, purchased, or used the product being recalled.

[21 CFR 7.41] Health hazard evaluation and recall classification.
(a) (a) An evaluation of the health hazard presented by a product being recalled or considered for recall will be conducted by an ad hoc committee of Food and Drug Administration scientists and will take into account, but need not be limited to, the following factors:
(a)(1) (1) Whether any disease or injuries have already occurred from the use of the product.
(a)(2) (2) Whether any existing conditions could contribute to a clinical situation that could expose humans or animals to a health hazard. Any conclusion shall be supported as completely as possible by scientific documentation and/or statements that the conclusion is the opinion of the individual(s) making the health hazard determination.
(a)(3) (3) Assessment of hazard to various segments of the population, e.g., children, surgical patients, pets, livestock, etc., who are expected to be exposed to the product being considered, with particular attention paid to the hazard to those individuals who may be at greatest risk.
(a)(4) (4) Assessment of the degree of seriousness of the health hazard to which the populations at risk would be exposed.
(a)(5) (5) Assessment of the likelihood of occurrence of the hazard.
(a)(6) (6) Assessment of the consequences (immediate or long-range) of occurrence of the hazard.
(b) (b) On the basis of this determination, the Food and Drug Administration will assign the recall a classification, i.e., Class I, Class II, or Class III, to indicate the relative degree of health hazard of the product being recalled or considered for recall.

[21 CFR 7.42] Recall strategy.
(a) (a) General.
(a)(1) (1) A recall strategy that takes into account the following factors will be developed by the agency for a Food and Drug Administration-requested recall and by the recalling firm for a firm-initiated recall to suit the individual circumstances of the particular recall:
(a)(1)(i) (i) Results of health hazard evaluation.
(a)(1)(ii) (ii) Ease in identifying the product.
(a)(1)(iii) (iii) Degree to which the product's deficiency is obvious to the consumer or user.
(a)(1)(iv) (iv) Degree to which the product remains unused in the market-place.
(a)(1)(v) (v) Continued availability of essential products.
(a)(2) (2) The Food and Drug Administration will review the adequacy of a proposed recall strategy developed by a recalling firm and recommend changes as appropriate. A recalling firm should conduct the recall in accordance with an approved recall strategy but need not delay initiation of a recall pending review of its recall strategy.
(b) (b) Elements of a recall strategy. A recall strategy will address the following elements regarding the conduct of the recall:
(b)(1) (1) Depth of recall. Depending on the product's degree of hazard and extent of distribution, the recall strategy will specify the level in the distribution chain to which the recall is to extend, as follows:
(b)(1)(i) (i) Consumer or user level, which may vary with product, including any intermediate wholesale or retail level; or
(b)(1)(ii) (ii) Retail level, including any intermediate wholesale level; or
(b)(1)(iii) (iii) Wholesale level.
(b)(2) (2) Public warning. The purpose of a public warning is to alert the public that a product being recalled presents a serious hazard to health. It is reserved for urgent situations where other means for preventing use of the recalled product appear inadequate. The Food and Drug Administration in consultation with the recalling firm will ordinarily issue such publicity. The recalling firm that decides to issue its own public warning is requested to submit its proposed public warning and plan for distribution of the warning for review and comment by the Food and Drug Administration. The recall strategy will specify whether a public warning is needed and whether it will issue as:
(b)(2)(i) (i) General public warning through the general news media, either national or local as appropriate, or
(b)(2)(ii) (ii) Public warning through specialized news media, e.g., professional or trade press, or to specific segments of the population such as physicians, hospitals, etc.
(b)(3) (3) Effectiveness checks. The purpose of effectiveness checks is to verify that all consignees at the recall depth specified by the strategy have received notification about the recall and have taken appropriate action. The method for contacting consignees may be accomplished by personal visits, telephone calls, letters, or a combination thereof. A guide entitled “Methods for Conducting Recall Effectiveness Checks” that describes the use of these different methods is available upon request from the Dockets Management Staff (HFA-305), Food and Drug Administration, 5630 Fishers Lane, rm. 1061, Rockville, MD 20852. The recalling firm will ordinarily be responsible for conducting effectiveness checks, but the Food and Drug Administration will assist in this task where necessary and appropriate. The recall strategy will specify the method(s) to be used for and the level of effectiveness checks that will be conducted, as follows:
(b)(3)(i) (i) Level A—100 percent of the total number of consignees to be contacted;
(b)(3)(ii) (ii) Level B—Some percentage of the total number of consignees to be contacted, which percentage is to be determined on a case-by-case basis, but is greater that 10 percent and less than 100 percent of the total number of consignees;
(b)(3)(iii) (iii) Level C—10 percent of the total number of consignees to be contacted;
(b)(3)(iv) (iv) Level D—2 percent of the total number of consignees to be contacted; or
(b)(3)(v) (v) Level E—No effectiveness checks.

[21 CFR 7.46] Firm-initiated recall.
(a) (a) A firm may decide of its own volition and under any circumstances to remove or correct a distributed product. A firm that does so because it believes the product to be violative is requested to notify immediately the appropriate Food and Drug Administration district office listed in § 5.115 of this chapter. Such removal or correction will be considered a recall only if the Food and Drug Administration regards the product as involving a violation that is subject to legal action, e.g., seizure. In such cases, the firm will be asked to provide the Food and Drug Administration the following information:
(a)(1) (1) Identity of the product involved.
(a)(2) (2) Reason for the removal or correction and the date and circumstances under which the product deficiency or possible deficiency was discovered.
(a)(3) (3) Evaluation of the risk associated with the deficiency or possible deficiency.
(a)(4) (4) Total amount of such products produced and/or the timespan of the production.
(a)(5) (5) Total amount of such products estimated to be in distribution channels.
(a)(6) (6) Distribution information, including the number of direct accounts and, where necessary, the identity of the direct accounts.
(a)(7) (7) A copy of the firm's recall communication if any has issued, or a proposed communication if none has issued.
(a)(8) (8) Proposed strategy for conducting the recall.
(a)(9) (9) Name and telephone number of the firm official who should be contacted concerning the recall.
(b) (b) The Food and Drug Administration will review the information submitted, advise the firm of the assigned recall classification, recommend any appropriate changes in the firm's strategy for the recall, and advise the firm that its recall will be placed in the weekly FDA Enforcement Report. Pending this review, the firm need not delay initiation of its product removal or correction.
(c) (c) A firm may decide to recall a product when informed by the Food and Drug Administration that the agency has determined that the product in question violates the law, but the agency has not specifically requested a recall. The firm's action also is considered a firm-initiated recall and is subject to paragraphs (a) and (b) of this section.
(d) (d) A firm that initiates a removal or correction of its product which the firm believes is a market withdrawal should consult with the appropriate Food and Drug Administration district office when the reason for the removal or correction is not obvious or clearly understood but where it is apparent, e.g., because of complaints or adverse reactions regarding the product, that the product is deficient in some respect. In such cases, the Food and Drug Administration will assist the firm in determining the exact nature of the problem.
ideal_answer:
Part 7, subpart C governs recalls.

Recall classification. FDA assigns a numerical classification - I, II or III - indicating the relative degree of health hazard presented by the recalled product (21 CFR 7.3(m)). Class I is a situation in which there is a reasonable probability that use of, or exposure to, a violative product will cause serious adverse health consequences or death; Class II, where use may cause temporary or medically reversible adverse health consequences, or where the probability of serious adverse health consequences is remote; Class III, where use is not likely to cause adverse health consequences (7.3(m)(1) through (3)).

Health hazard evaluation. The classification rests on an evaluation conducted by an ad hoc committee of FDA scientists, taking into account whether disease or injury has already occurred, whether existing conditions could expose humans or animals to a health hazard, the hazard to population segments including those at greatest risk, the seriousness of the hazard, its likelihood of occurrence, and its immediate or long-range consequences (7.41(a)(1) through (6)); on that basis FDA assigns the Class I, II or III designation (7.41(b)).

Recall strategy. A recall strategy is developed by FDA for an agency-requested recall and by the recalling firm for a firm-initiated recall, taking into account the health hazard evaluation, ease of identifying the product, how obvious the deficiency is to the consumer or user, how much product remains unused in the marketplace, and continued availability of essential products (7.42(a)(1)). It addresses three elements (7.42(b)):
- Depth of recall - the level in the distribution chain to which the recall extends: consumer or user level, retail level, or wholesale level (7.42(b)(1)).
- Public warning - to alert the public that the product presents a serious hazard to health, reserved for urgent situations where other means of preventing use appear inadequate, issued through general news media or specialized news media (7.42(b)(2)).
- Effectiveness checks - to verify that consignees at the specified depth received notification and took appropriate action, at Level A (100 percent of consignees) through Level E (no effectiveness checks) (7.42(b)(3)).

Firm-initiated recall. A firm may remove or correct a distributed product of its own volition and under any circumstances. Where it does so because it believes the product violative, it is requested to notify the appropriate FDA district office immediately and to provide the identity of the product; the reason for the removal or correction and the date and circumstances of discovery; an evaluation of the risk; the total amount produced and the timespan of production; the amount estimated to be in distribution channels; distribution information; a copy of any recall communication; the proposed recall strategy; and the name and telephone number of the firm official to contact (7.46(a)(1) through (9)). FDA then reviews the submission, advises the firm of the assigned classification, recommends any changes to the strategy, and advises that the recall will be listed in the weekly FDA Enforcement Report (7.46(b)).

question: What controls are required for closed systems under Part 11?
evidence:
[21 CFR 11.10] Controls for closed systems.
— Persons who use closed systems to create, modify, maintain, or transmit electronic records shall employ procedures and controls designed to ensure the authenticity, integrity, and, when appropriate, the confidentiality of electronic records, and to ensure that the signer cannot readily repudiate the signed record as not genuine. Such procedures and controls shall include the following:
(a) (a) Validation of systems to ensure accuracy, reliability, consistent intended performance, and the ability to discern invalid or altered records.
(b) (b) The ability to generate accurate and complete copies of records in both human readable and electronic form suitable for inspection, review, and copying by the agency. Persons should contact the agency if there are any questions regarding the ability of the agency to perform such review and copying of the electronic records.
(c) (c) Protection of records to enable their accurate and ready retrieval throughout the records retention period.
(d) (d) Limiting system access to authorized individuals.
(e) (e) Use of secure, computer-generated, time-stamped audit trails to independently record the date and time of operator entries and actions that create, modify, or delete electronic records. Record changes shall not obscure previously recorded information. Such audit trail documentation shall be retained for a period at least as long as that required for the subject electronic records and shall be available for agency review and copying.
(f) (f) Use of operational system checks to enforce permitted sequencing of steps and events, as appropriate.
(g) (g) Use of authority checks to ensure that only authorized individuals can use the system, electronically sign a record, access the operation or computer system input or output device, alter a record, or perform the operation at hand.
(h) (h) Use of device (e.g., terminal) checks to determine, as appropriate, the validity of the source of data input or operational instruction.
(i) (i) Determination that persons who develop, maintain, or use electronic record/electronic signature systems have the education, training, and experience to perform their assigned tasks.
(j) (j) The establishment of, and adherence to, written policies that hold individuals accountable and responsible for actions initiated under their electronic signatures, in order to deter record and signature falsification.
(k) (k) Use of appropriate controls over systems documentation including:
(k)(1) (1) Adequate controls over the distribution of, access to, and use of documentation for system operation and maintenance.
(k)(2) (2) Revision and change control procedures to maintain an audit trail that documents time-sequenced development and modification of systems documentation.

question: What is the scope of 21 CFR Part 820 and which manufacturers are subject to it?
evidence:
[21 CFR 820.1] Scope.
(a) (a) Applicability. Current good manufacturing practice (CGMP) requirements are set forth in this quality management system regulation (QMSR). The requirements in this part govern the methods used in, and the facilities and controls used for, the design, manufacture, packaging, labeling, storage, installation, and servicing of all finished devices intended for human use. The requirements in this part are intended to assure that finished devices will be safe and effective and otherwise in compliance with the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and that the use of other terminology, such as “safety and performance,” in this part does not change this statutory standard or the requirements of this part. Any manufacturers engaged in the design, manufacture, packaging, labeling, storage, installation, or servicing of a finished device must establish and maintain a quality management system that is appropriate for its specific device(s). Manufacturers subject to this part include, but are not limited to, manufacturers that perform the functions of contract sterilization, installation, relabeling, remanufacturing, repacking, or specification development, as well as initial distributors of foreign entities that perform these functions. If a manufacturer engages in only some operations subject to the requirements in this part, and not in others, that manufacturer need only comply with those requirements applicable to the operations in which it is engaged.
(a)(1) (1) Finished devices. The provisions of this part shall apply to any finished device, as defined in this part, intended for human use, that is manufactured in any State or Territory of the United States, the District of Columbia, or the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or that is imported or offered for import into the United States.
(a)(2) (2) Components or parts. The provisions of this part do not apply to manufacturers of components or parts of finished devices, but such manufacturers are encouraged to consider provisions of this regulation as appropriate.
(a)(3) (3) Blood and blood components. The provisions of this part do not apply to manufacturers of blood and blood components used for transfusion or for further manufacturing. Such manufacturers are subject to subchapter F of this chapter.
(a)(4) (4) HCT/Ps. The provisions of this part apply to manufacturers of human cells, tissues, and cellular and tissue-based products (HCT/Ps), as defined in § 1271.3(d) of this chapter, that are devices (subject to premarket review or notification, or exempt from notification, under an application submitted under the device provisions of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act or under a biological product license application under section 351 of the Public Health Service Act). HCT/Ps regulated as devices are also subject to the donor-eligibility requirements set forth in part 1271, subpart C of this chapter and applicable current good tissue practice requirements in part 1271, subpart D of this chapter. In the event of a conflict between applicable regulations in part 1271 and in other parts of this chapter, the regulation specifically applicable to the device in question shall supersede the more general regulation.
(b) (b) Conflicts with other requirements under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. The QMSR for devices in this part supplements regulations in other parts of this chapter except where explicitly stated otherwise. To the extent that any applicable requirements in this part conflict with requirements in other parts of this chapter, the requirements specifically applicable to the device in question shall supersede the more generally applicable requirements. Moreover, to the extent that any clauses of ISO 13485 (incorporated by reference, see § 820.7) conflict with any provisions of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and/or its other implementing regulations, the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and/or its other implementing regulations will control.
(c) (c) Foreign manufacturers. A device that is imported or offered for import into the United States is subject to refusal of admission to the United States under section 801(a) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act if, among other things, it appears to be adulterated as set forth in the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and its implementing regulations.
(d) (d) Exemptions or variances.
(d)(1) (1) A manufacturer subject to any requirement under section 520(f)(1) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, including any requirements under this part, may petition for an exemption or variance from such requirement in accordance with section 520(f)(2) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. Petitions for an exemption or variance shall be submitted in accordance with the procedures set forth in § 10.30 of this chapter.
(d)(2) (2) FDA may initiate and grant a variance from any requirement(s) in this part when the Agency determines that such variance is in the best interest of the public health, including that there is a public health need for the device and the device would not likely be made sufficiently available without the variance. Such variance will remain in effect only so long as there remains a public health need for the device and the device would not likely be made sufficiently available without the variance.

[21 CFR 820.10] Requirements for a quality management system.
— A manufacturer subject to this part as described by § 820.1(a) must:
(a) (a) Document. Document a quality management system that complies with the applicable requirements of ISO 13485 (incorporated by reference, see § 820.7) and other applicable requirements of this part; and
(b) (b) Applicable regulatory requirements. Comply, as appropriate, with the other applicable regulatory requirements in this title, including, but not limited to the following, to fully comply with the listed ISO 13485 Clause:
(b)(1) (1) For Clause 7.5.8 in ISO 13485, Identification, the manufacturer must document a system to assign unique device identification to the medical device in accordance with the requirements of part 830 of this chapter.
(b)(2) (2) For Clause 7.5.9.1 in ISO 13485, Traceability—General, the manufacturer must document procedures for traceability in accordance with the requirements of part 821 of this chapter, if applicable.
(b)(3) (3) For Clause 8.2.3 in ISO 13485, Reporting to regulatory authorities, the manufacturer must notify FDA of complaints that meet the reporting criteria of part 803 of this chapter.
(b)(4) (4) For Clauses 7.2.3, 8.2.3, and 8.3.3, advisory notices shall be handled in accordance with the requirements of part 806 of this chapter.
(c) (c) Design and development. Manufacturers of class II, class III, and those class I devices listed in paragraph (c)(1) of this section and table 1 to paragraph (c)(2) of this section must comply with the requirements in Design and Development, Clause 7.3 and its Subclauses in ISO 13485. The class I devices are as follows:
(c)(1) (1) Devices automated with computer software; and
(c)(2) (2) The devices listed in the following table:
(d) (d) Devices that support or sustain life. Manufacturers of devices that support or sustain life, the failure of which to perform when properly used in accordance with instructions for use provided in the labeling can be reasonably expected to result in a significant injury, must comply with the requirements in Traceability for Implantable Devices, Clause 7.5.9.2 in ISO 13485, in addition to all other applicable requirements in this part, as appropriate.

Any manufacturer engaged in the design, manufacture, packaging, labeling, storage, installation or servicing of a finished device must establish and maintain a quality management system appropriate for its specific device(s), and must document a quality management system complying with the applicable requirements of ISO 13485 (incorporated by reference at 820.7) and the other applicable requirements of the part (820.1(a); 820.10(a)). Manufacturers subject to the part include, but are not limited to, those performing contract sterilization, installation, relabeling, remanufacturing, repacking or specification development, as well as initial distributors of foreign entities performing those functions. A manufacturer engaged in only some of the operations subject to the part need only comply with the requirements applicable to the operations in which it is engaged (820.1(a)).

Applicability and carve-outs (820.1(a)(1) through (4)). The part applies to any finished device intended for human use manufactured in a State or Territory of the United States, the District of Columbia or Puerto Rico, or imported or offered for import. It does not apply to manufacturers of components or parts of finished devices, though they are encouraged to consider its provisions as appropriate. It does not apply to manufacturers of blood and blood components used for transfusion or further manufacturing, who are subject to subchapter F. It does apply to manufacturers of HCT/Ps, as defined in 1271.3(d), that are devices.

The QMSR supplements regulations in other parts of this chapter except where explicitly stated otherwise (820.1(b)).

(a)(2) (2) A standardized review process or procedure for determining when an event meets the criteria for reporting under this part; and
(a)(3) (3) Timely transmission of complete medical device reports to manufacturers or to us, or to both if required.
(b) (b) Documentation and recordkeeping requirements for:
(b)(1) (1) Information that was evaluated to determine if an event was reportable;
(b)(2) (2) All medical device reports and information submitted to manufacturers and/or us;
(b)(3) (3) Any information that was evaluated for the purpose of preparing the submission of annual reports; and
(b)(4) (4) Systems that ensure access to information that facilitates timely followup and inspection by us.

[21 CFR 803.18] What are the requirements for establishing and maintaining MDR files or records that apply to me?
(a) (a) If you are a user facility, importer, or manufacturer, you must establish and maintain MDR event files. You must clearly identify all MDR event files and maintain them to facilitate timely access.
(b)(1) (b)(1) For purposes of this part, “MDR event files” are written or electronic files maintained by user facilities, importers, and manufacturers. MDR event files may incorporate references to other information (e.g., medical records, patient files, engineering reports), in lieu of copying and maintaining duplicates in this file. Your MDR event files must contain:
(b)(1)(i) (i) Information in your possession or references to information related to the adverse event, including all documentation of your deliberations and decision making processes used to determine if a device-related death, serious injury, or malfunction was or was not reportable under this part;
(b)(1)(ii) (ii) Copies of all reports submitted under this part (whether paper or electronic), and of all other information related to the event that you submitted to us or other entities such as an importer, distributor, or manufacturer; and
(b)(1)(iii) (iii) Copies of all electronic acknowledgments FDA sends you in response to electronic MDR submissions.
(b)(2) (2) If you are a user facility, importer, or manufacturer, you must permit any authorized FDA employee, at all reasonable times, to access, to copy, and to verify the records required by this part.
(c) (c) If you are a user facility, you must retain an MDR event file relating to an adverse event for a period of 2 years from the date of the event. If you are a manufacturer or importer, you must retain an MDR event file relating to an adverse event for a period of 2 years from the date of the event or a period of time equivalent to the expected life of the device, whichever is greater. If the device is no longer distributed, you still must maintain MDR event files for the time periods described in this paragraph (c).
(d)(1) (d)(1) If you are a device distributor, you must establish and maintain device complaint records (files). ideal_answer:
Written MDR procedures (21 CFR 803.17). A user facility, importer or manufacturer must develop, maintain and implement written MDR procedures covering: internal systems providing for timely and effective identification, communication and evaluation of events that may be subject to MDR requirements; a standardized review process or procedure for determining when an event meets the reporting criteria of this part; and timely transmission of complete medical device reports to manufacturers or to FDA, or both where required (803.17(a)(1) through (3)). The procedures must also cover documentation and recordkeeping for the information evaluated to determine whether an event was reportable, all reports and information submitted to manufacturers or FDA, any information evaluated in preparing annual reports, and systems ensuring access to information that facilitates timely follow-up and inspection (803.17(b)(1) through (4)).

MDR files and records (803.18). A user facility, importer or manufacturer must establish and maintain MDR event files, clearly identified and maintained to facilitate timely access (803.18(a)). MDR event files are written or electronic files that may incorporate references to other information in lieu of copying it, and must contain information or references relating to the adverse event, including all documentation of the deliberations and decision-making used to determine whether a device-related death, serious injury or malfunction was reportable; copies of all reports submitted under this part and other information about the event submitted to FDA or to an importer, distributor or manufacturer; and copies of all electronic acknowledgments FDA sends in response to electronic submissions (803.18(b)(1)(i) through (iii)). Authorized FDA employees must be permitted at all reasonable times to access, copy and verify the records (803.18(b)(2)).

Retention. A user facility must retain an MDR event file relating to an adverse event for 2 years from the date of the event. A manufacturer or importer must retain it for 2 years from the date of the event or for a period equivalent to the expected life of the device, whichever is greater (803.18(c)). A device distributor must establish and maintain device complaint records and retain them for 2 years from the date the record was included in the file, or for a period equivalent to the expected life of the device, whichever is greater (803.18(d)(1) and (2)). A manufacturer may maintain MDR event files as part of its part 820 complaint file provided the records are prominently identified as MDR reportable events (803.18(e)).

question: What CGMP requirements apply to personnel under Part 117 Subpart B?
evidence:
[21 CFR 117.10] Personnel.
— The management of the establishment must take reasonable measures and precautions to ensure the following:
(a) (a) Disease control. Any person who, by medical examination or supervisory observation, is shown to have, or appears to have, an illness, open lesion, including boils, sores, or infected wounds, or any other abnormal source of microbial contamination by which there is a reasonable possibility of food, food-contact surfaces, or food-packaging materials becoming contaminated, must be excluded from any operations which may be expected to result in such contamination until the condition is corrected, unless conditions such as open lesions, boils, and infected wounds are adequately covered (e.g., by an impermeable cover). Personnel must be instructed to report such health conditions to their supervisors.
(b) (b) Cleanliness. All persons working in direct contact with food, food-contact surfaces, and food-packaging materials must conform to hygienic practices while on duty to the extent necessary to protect against allergen cross-contact and against contamination of food. The methods for maintaining cleanliness include:
(b)(1) (1) Wearing outer garments suitable to the operation in a manner that protects against allergen cross-contact and against the contamination of food, food-contact surfaces, or food-packaging materials.
(b)(2) (2) Maintaining adequate personal cleanliness.
(b)(3) (3) Washing hands thoroughly (and sanitizing if necessary to protect against contamination with undesirable microorganisms) in an adequate hand-washing facility before starting work, after each absence from the work station, and at any other time when the hands may have become soiled or contaminated.
(b)(4) (4) Removing all unsecured jewelry and other objects that might fall into food, equipment, or containers, and removing hand jewelry that cannot be adequately sanitized during periods in which food is manipulated by hand. If such hand jewelry cannot be removed, it may be covered by material which can be maintained in an intact, clean, and sanitary condition and which effectively protects against the contamination by these objects of the food, food-contact surfaces, or food-packaging materials.
(b)(5) (5) Maintaining gloves, if they are used in food handling, in an intact, clean, and sanitary condition.
(b)(6) (6) Wearing, where appropriate, in an effective manner, hair nets, headbands, caps, beard covers, or other effective hair restraints.
(b)(7) (7) Storing clothing or other personal belongings in areas other than where food is exposed or where equipment or utensils are washed.
(b)(8) (8) Confining the following to areas other than where food may be exposed or where equipment or utensils are washed: eating food, chewing gum, drinking beverages, or using tobacco.
(b)(9) (9) Taking any other necessary precautions to protect against allergen cross-contact and against contamination of food, food-contact surfaces, or food-packaging materials with microorganisms or foreign substances (including perspiration, hair, cosmetics, tobacco, chemicals, and medicines applied to the skin).

Part 606 sets the CGMP requirements for blood and blood components in three areas relevant here.

Personnel (21 CFR 606.20). The personnel responsible for the collection, processing, compatibility testing, storage or distribution of blood or blood components must be adequate in number, educational background, training and experience, including professional training as necessary, or a combination thereof (606.20(b)). Persons whose presence can adversely affect the safety and purity of the products must be excluded from areas where those activities are conducted (606.20(c)).

Standard operating procedures (606.100). Establishments must establish, maintain and follow written standard operating procedures for all steps in the collection, processing, compatibility testing, storage and distribution of blood and blood components for allogeneic transfusion, autologous transfusion and further manufacturing (606.100(b)). The enumerated procedures include donor eligibility criteria including acceptable medical history; methods of performing donor qualifying tests and measurements with minimum and maximum values where these determine acceptability; phlebotomy site preparation; accurately relating the product to the donor; the blood collection procedure with in-process precautions for measuring the quantity removed; component preparation including time restrictions; all tests and repeat tests during manufacturing; pretransfusion testing with precautions for identifying recipient samples and crossmatched units; investigation of adverse donor and recipient reactions; storage temperatures and their control as prescribed in 600.15 and 610.53; expiration dates as prescribed in 610.53; criteria for reissue of returned blood; relating a unit to its final disposition; quality control of supplies and reagents; equipment maintenance and calibration schedules; labeling procedures with safeguards against mixups; apheresis procedures; and procedures for recovered plasma. In all instances except clinical investigations, the procedures must comply with the additional standards in part 640 for the products being processed (606.100(a)).

Look-back (606.100(b)(19)). Procedures under 610.46 and 610.47 are required to identify previously donated blood and blood components from a donor who later tests reactive for evidence of HIV or HCV infection under 610.40, or where the establishment is made aware of other reliable test results; to quarantine in-date blood and components previously donated by such a donor that are intended for use in another person or for further manufacture into injectable products, subject to the stated exception for pooled components; to notify consignees to quarantine such units; and to determine the suitability of quarantined in-date units for release, destruction or relabeling.

Records (606.160). Records must be maintained concurrently with the performance of each significant step in the collection, processing, compatibility testing, storage and distribution of each unit, so that all steps can be clearly traced; they must be legible and indelible and must identify the person performing the work (606.160(a)(1)). Records must be available from which to determine lot numbers of supplies and reagents used for specific lots or units of the final product (606.160(a)(2)). A donor number must be assigned to each accepted donor, relating the unit collected to that donor, to the medical record, to any component or product from that unit, and to all records of its history and ultimate disposition (606.160(c)).

Retention. Records must be retained for such interval beyond the expiration date of the blood or blood component as necessary to facilitate reporting of any unfavourable clinical reactions, and individual product records must be retained no less than 10 years after the records of processing are completed or 6 months after the latest expiration date for the individual product, whichever is the later date (606.160(d)).

question: What holding and distribution requirements apply under Part 211?
evidence:
[21 CFR 211.142] Warehousing procedures.
— Written procedures describing the warehousing of drug products shall be established and followed. They shall include:
(a) (a) Quarantine of drug products before release by the quality control unit.
(b) (b) Storage of drug products under appropriate conditions of temperature, humidity, and light so that the identity, strength, quality, and purity of the drug products are not affected.

[21 CFR 211.150] Distribution procedures.
— Written procedures shall be established, and followed, describing the distribution of drug products. They shall include:
(a) (a) A procedure whereby the oldest approved stock of a drug product is distributed first. Deviation from this requirement is permitted if such deviation is temporary and appropriate.
(b) (b) A system by which the distribution of each lot of drug product can be readily determined to facilitate its recall if necessary.

[21 CFR 117.20] Plant and grounds.
(a) (a) Grounds. The grounds about a food plant under the control of the operator must be kept in a condition that will protect against the contamination of food. The methods for adequate maintenance of grounds must include:
(a)(1) (1) Properly storing equipment, removing litter and waste, and cutting weeds or grass within the immediate vicinity of the plant that may constitute an attractant, breeding place, or harborage for pests.
(a)(2) (2) Maintaining roads, yards, and parking lots so that they do not constitute a source of contamination in areas where food is exposed.
(a)(3) (3) Adequately draining areas that may contribute contamination to food by seepage, foot-borne filth, or providing a breeding place for pests.
(a)(4) (4) Operating systems for waste treatment and disposal in an adequate manner so that they do not constitute a source of contamination in areas where food is exposed.
(a)(5) (5) If the plant grounds are bordered by grounds not under the operator's control and not maintained in the manner described in paragraphs (a)(1) through (4) of this section, care must be exercised in the plant by inspection, extermination, or other means to exclude pests, dirt, and filth that may be a source of food contamination.
(b) (b) Plant construction and design. The plant must be suitable in size, construction, and design to facilitate maintenance and sanitary operations for food-production purposes (i.e., manufacturing, processing, packing, and holding). The plant must:
(b)(1) (1) Provide adequate space for such placement of equipment and storage of materials as is necessary for maintenance, sanitary operations, and the production of safe food.
(b)(2) (2) Permit the taking of adequate precautions to reduce the potential for allergen cross-contact and for contamination of food, food-contact surfaces, or food-packaging materials with microorganisms, chemicals, filth, and other extraneous material. (b)(3) (3) Permit the taking of adequate precautions to protect food in installed outdoor bulk vessels by any effective means, including:
(b)(3)(i) (i) Using protective coverings.
(b)(3)(ii) (ii) Controlling areas over and around the vessels to eliminate harborages for pests.
(b)(3)(iii) (iii) Checking on a regular basis for pests and pest infestation.
(b)(3)(iv) (iv) Skimming fermentation vessels, as necessary.

[21 CFR 117.35] Sanitary operations.
(a) (a) General maintenance. Buildings, fixtures, and other physical facilities of the plant must be maintained in a clean and sanitary condition and must be kept in repair adequate to prevent food from becoming adulterated. Cleaning and sanitizing of utensils and equipment must be conducted in a manner that protects against allergen cross-contact and against contamination of food, food-contact surfaces, or food-packaging materials.
(b) (b) Substances used in cleaning and sanitizing; storage of toxic materials.
(b)(1) (1) Cleaning compounds and sanitizing agents used in cleaning and sanitizing procedures must be free from undesirable microorganisms and must be safe and adequate under the conditions of use. Only the following toxic materials may be used or stored in a plant where food is processed or exposed:
(b)(1)(i) (i) Those required to maintain clean and sanitary conditions;
(b)(1)(ii) (ii) Those necessary for use in laboratory testing procedures;
(b)(1)(iii) (iii) Those necessary for plant and equipment maintenance and operation; and
(b)(1)(iv) (iv) Those necessary for use in the plant's operations.
(b)(2) (2) Toxic cleaning compounds, sanitizing agents, and pesticide chemicals must be identified, held, and stored in a manner that protects against contamination of food, food-contact surfaces, or food-packaging materials.

question: Which parts of Title 21 govern device establishment registration, listing, and unique device identification, and how do they interact with Part 820?
ideal_answer:
Three different parts, each doing a different job, with Part 820 providing the quality-system hooks into two of them.

Establishment registration and device listing - Part 807. An owner or operator of an establishment not exempt under section 510(g) of the Act or subpart D of Part 807, engaged in the manufacture, preparation, propagation, compounding, assembly or processing of a device intended for human use, must register and submit a device list (21 CFR 807.20(a)). The duty expressly reaches those who initiate or develop specifications for a device to be manufactured by a second party, sterilize or otherwise make a device for or on behalf of a specifications developer, repackage or relabel a device, reprocess a single-use device previously used on a patient, act as an initial importer as defined in 807.3(g), and manufacture components or accessories ready to be used for a health-related purpose and packaged or labeled for commercial distribution for that purpose (807.20(a)(1) through (6)).

Unique device identification - Part 830. A UDI must be issued under a system operated by FDA or an FDA-accredited issuing agency; conform to ISO/IEC 15459-2, 15459-4 and 15459-6, each incorporated by reference at 830.10; and use only characters and numbers from the invariant character set of ISO/IEC 646, also incorporated at 830.10 (830.20(a) through (c)).

How Part 820 interacts. Part 820 does not itself set the registration, listing or UDI requirements; it requires the quality management system to reach them. Under 820.10(b), a manufacturer must comply, as appropriate, with the other applicable regulatory requirements in Title 21 in order to fully comply with the listed ISO 13485 clauses - and specifically, for Clause 7.5.8, Identification, must document a system to assign unique device identification to the medical device in accordance with the requirements of part 830 (820.10(b)(1)). On the records side, 820.35(c) provides that, in addition to the requirements of Clauses 7.5.1, 7.5.8 and 7.5.9 in ISO 13485, the UDI must be recorded for each medical device or batch of medical devices.

So: Part 807 is the registration and listing regime, Part 830 sets what a UDI must be, and Part 820 requires the manufacturer to document the assignment system in accordance with Part 830 (820.10(b)(1)) and to record the UDI (820.35(c)). Part 820 contains no registration or listing requirement of its own.

context.text:

(a) (a) Document. Document a quality management system that complies with the applicable requirements of ISO 13485 (incorporated by reference, see § 820.7) and other applicable requirements of this part; and
(b) (b) Applicable regulatory requirements. Comply, as appropriate, with the other applicable regulatory requirements in this title, including, but not limited to the following, to fully comply with the listed ISO 13485 Clause:
(b)(1) (1) For Clause 7.5.8 in ISO 13485, Identification, the manufacturer must document a system to assign unique device identification to the medical device in accordance with the requirements of part 830 of this chapter.
(b)(2) (2) For Clause 7.5.9.1 in ISO 13485, Traceability—General, the manufacturer must document procedures for traceability in accordance with the requirements of part 821 of this chapter, if applicable.
(b)(3) (3) For Clause 8.2.3 in ISO 13485, Reporting to regulatory authorities, the manufacturer must notify FDA of complaints that meet the reporting criteria of part 803 of this chapter.
(b)(4) (4) For Clauses 7.2.3, 8.2.3, and 8.3.3, advisory notices shall be handled in accordance with the requirements of part 806 of this chapter.
(c) (c) Design and development. Manufacturers of class II, class III, and those class I devices listed in paragraph (c)(1) of this section and table 1 to paragraph (c)(2) of this section must comply with the requirements in Design and Development, Clause 7.3 and its Subclauses in ISO 13485. (c)(1) (1) Devices automated with computer software; and

(d) (d) Devices that support or sustain life. Manufacturers of devices that support or sustain life, the failure of which to perform when properly used in accordance with instructions for use provided in the labeling can be reasonably expected to result in a significant injury, must comply with the requirements in Traceability for Implantable Devices, Clause 7.5.9.2 in ISO 13485, in addition to all other applicable requirements in this part, as appropriate.

question: Are human cells, tissues, and cellular and tissue-based products regulated as devices subject to Part 820, and what else applies to them?
evidence:
[21 CFR 820.1] Scope.
(a) (a) Applicability. Current good manufacturing practice (CGMP) requirements are set forth in this quality management system regulation (QMSR). The requirements in this part govern the methods used in, and the facilities and controls used for, the design, manufacture, packaging, labeling, storage, installation, and servicing of all finished devices intended for human use. The requirements in this part are intended to assure that finished devices will be safe and effective and otherwise in compliance with the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and that the use of other terminology, such as “safety and performance,” in this part does not change this statutory standard or the requirements of this part. Any manufacturers engaged in the design, manufacture, packaging, labeling, storage, installation, or servicing of a finished device must establish and maintain a quality management system that is appropriate for its specific device(s). Manufacturers subject to this part include, but are not limited to, manufacturers that perform the functions of contract sterilization, installation, relabeling, remanufacturing, repacking, or specification development, as well as initial distributors of foreign entities that perform these functions. If a manufacturer engages in only some operations subject to the requirements in this part, and not in others, that manufacturer need only comply with those requirements applicable to the operations in which it is engaged.
(a)(1) (1) Finished devices. The provisions of this part shall apply to any finished device, as defined in this part, intended for human use, that is manufactured in any State or Territory of the United States, the District of Columbia, or the Commonwealth of Puerto Rico, or that is imported or offered for import into the United States.
(a)(2) (2) Components or parts. The provisions of this part do not apply to manufacturers of components or parts of finished devices, but such manufacturers are encouraged to consider provisions of this regulation as appropriate.
(a)(3) (3) Blood and blood components. The provisions of this part do not apply to manufacturers of blood and blood components used for transfusion or for further manufacturing. Such manufacturers are subject to subchapter F of this chapter.
(a)(4) (4) HCT/Ps. The provisions of this part apply to manufacturers of human cells, tissues, and cellular and tissue-based products (HCT/Ps), as defined in § 1271.3(d) of this chapter, that are devices (subject to premarket review or notification, or exempt from notification, under an application submitted under the device provisions of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act or under a biological product license application under section 351 of the Public Health Service Act). HCT/Ps regulated as devices are also subject to the donor-eligibility requirements set forth in part 1271, subpart C of this chapter and applicable current good tissue practice requirements in part 1271, subpart D of this chapter. In the event of a conflict between applicable regulations in part 1271 and in other parts of this chapter, the regulation specifically applicable to the device in question shall supersede the more general regulation.
(b) (b) Conflicts with other requirements under the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. The QMSR for devices in this part supplements regulations in other parts of this chapter except where explicitly stated otherwise. To the extent that any applicable requirements in this part conflict with requirements in other parts of this chapter, the requirements specifically applicable to the device in question shall supersede the more generally applicable requirements. Moreover, to the extent that any clauses of ISO 13485 (incorporated by reference, see § 820.7) conflict with any provisions of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and/or its other implementing regulations, the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and/or its other implementing regulations will control.
(c) (c) Foreign manufacturers. A device that is imported or offered for import into the United States is subject to refusal of admission to the United States under section 801(a) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act if, among other things, it appears to be adulterated as set forth in the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act and its implementing regulations.
(d) (d) Exemptions or variances.
(d)(1) (1) A manufacturer subject to any requirement under section 520(f)(1) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act, including any requirements under this part, may petition for an exemption or variance from such requirement in accordance with section 520(f)(2) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. Petitions for an exemption or variance shall be submitted in accordance with the procedures set forth in § 10.30 of this chapter.
(d)(2) (2) FDA may initiate and grant a variance from any requirement(s) in this part when the Agency determines that such variance is in the best interest of the public health, including that there is a public health need for the device and the device would not likely be made sufficiently available without the variance. Such variance will remain in effect only so long as there remains a public health need for the device and the device would not likely be made sufficiently available without the variance.
ideal_answer:
Yes. The provisions of Part 820 apply to manufacturers of human cells, tissues, and cellular and tissue-based products (HCT/Ps), as defined in 21 CFR 1271.3(d), that are devices - that is, devices subject to premarket review or notification, or exempt from notification (21 CFR 820.1(a)(4)).

What else applies: such HCT/Ps remain subject to Part 1271, the regulations for human cells, tissues, and cellular and tissue-based products, so both sets of requirements are engaged.

How the two interact: the QMSR in Part 820 supplements the regulations in other parts of this chapter except where explicitly stated otherwise, and to the extent that a requirement in Part 820 conflicts with a requirement elsewhere, the regulation specifically applicable to the device in question supersedes the more general (820.1(b)). So where Part 1271 speaks specifically to an HCT/P, it governs over the more general Part 820 provision.

Note the contrast with the neighbouring carve-outs in the same paragraph: Part 820 does not apply to manufacturers of components or parts of finished devices (820.1(a)(2)), nor to manufacturers of blood and blood components used for transfusion or further manufacturing, who are subject to subchapter F (820.1(a)(3)). HCT/Ps that are devices are in scope, not carved out.

question: How must advisory notices be handled under Part 820, and which section establishes that requirement?
evidence:
[21 CFR 820.10] Requirements for a quality management system.
— A manufacturer subject to this part as described by § 820.1(a) must:
(a) (a) Document. Document a quality management system that complies with the applicable requirements of ISO 13485 (incorporated by reference, see § 820.7) and other applicable requirements of this part; and
(b) (b) Applicable regulatory requirements. Comply, as appropriate, with the other applicable regulatory requirements in this title, including, but not limited to the following, to fully comply with the listed ISO 13485 Clause:
(b)(1) (1) For Clause 7.5.8 in ISO 13485, Identification, the manufacturer must document a system to assign unique device identification to the medical device in accordance with the requirements of part 830 of this chapter.
(b)(2) (2) For Clause 7.5.9.1 in ISO 13485, Traceability—General, the manufacturer must document procedures for traceability in accordance with the requirements of part 821 of this chapter, if applicable.
(b)(3) (3) For Clause 8.2.3 in ISO 13485, Reporting to regulatory authorities, the manufacturer must notify FDA of complaints that meet the reporting criteria of part 803 of this chapter.
(b)(4) (4) For Clauses 7.2.3, 8.2.3, and 8.3.3, advisory notices shall be handled in accordance with the requirements of part 806 of this chapter.
(c) (c) Design and development. Manufacturers of class II, class III, and those class I devices listed in paragraph (c)(1) of this section and table 1 to paragraph (c)(2) of this section must comply with the requirements in Design and Development, Clause 7.3 and its Subclauses in ISO 13485. The class I devices are as follows:
(c)(1) (1) Devices automated with computer software; and
(c)(2) (2) The devices listed in the following table:
(d) (d) Devices that support or sustain life. Manufacturers of devices that support or sustain life, the failure of which to perform when properly used in accordance with instructions for use provided in the labeling can be reasonably expected to result in a significant injury, must comply with the requirements in Traceability for Implantable Devices, Clause 7.5.9.2 in ISO 13485, in addition to all other applicable requirements in this part, as appropriate.
(e) (e) Enforcement. The failure to comply with any applicable requirement in this part renders a device adulterated under section 501(h) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. Such a device, as well as any person responsible for the failure to comply, is subject to regulatory action.
ideal_answer:
The requirement is established by 21 CFR 820.10(b)(4): for Clauses 7.2.3, 8.2.3 and 8.3.3 in ISO 13485, advisory notices shall be handled in accordance with the requirements of part 806 of this chapter.

So advisory notices are not handled under Part 820's own machinery. 820.10(b)(4) routes them to Part 806, Medical Devices; Reports of Corrections and Removals, and it is Part 806's requirements that govern how the notice is handled and reported.

This sits within 820.10(b), which obliges a manufacturer to comply, as appropriate, with the other applicable regulatory requirements in Title 21 in order to fully comply with the listed ISO 13485 clauses.

question: Under Part 111, what is the difference between the responsibilities of quality control personnel and those of production personnel?

context.heading: What must quality control personnel do?

question: What is the difference between a process preventive control, a sanitation preventive control, and an allergen preventive control under Part 117?
evidence:
[21 CFR 117.135] Preventive controls.
(a)(1) (a)(1) You must identify and implement preventive controls to provide assurances that any hazards requiring a preventive control will be significantly minimized or prevented and the food manufactured, processed, packed, or held by your facility will not be adulterated under section 402 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act or misbranded under section 403(w) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.
(a)(2) (2) Preventive controls required by paragraph (a)(1) of this section include:
(a)(2)(i) (i) Controls at critical control points (CCPs), if there are any CCPs; and
(a)(2)(ii) (ii) Controls, other than those at CCPs, that are also appropriate for food safety.
(b) (b) Preventive controls must be written.
(c) (c) Preventive controls include, as appropriate to the facility and the food:
(c)(1) (1) Process controls. Process controls include procedures, practices, and processes to ensure the control of parameters during operations such as heat processing, acidifying, irradiating, and refrigerating foods. Process controls must include, as appropriate to the nature of the applicable control and its role in the facility's food safety system:
(c)(1)(i) (i) Parameters associated with the control of the hazard; and
(c)(1)(ii) (ii) The maximum or minimum value, or combination of values, to which any biological, chemical, or physical parameter must be controlled to significantly minimize or prevent a hazard requiring a process control.
(c)(2) (2) Food allergen controls. Food allergen controls include procedures, practices, and processes to control food allergens. Food allergen controls must include those procedures, practices, and processes employed for:
(c)(2)(i) (i) Ensuring protection of food from allergen cross-contact, including during storage, handling, and use; and
(c)(2)(ii) (ii) Labeling the finished food, including ensuring that the finished food is not misbranded under section 403(w) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.
(c)(3) (3) Sanitation controls. Sanitation controls include procedures, practices, and processes to ensure that the facility is maintained in a sanitary condition adequate to significantly minimize or prevent hazards such as environmental pathogens, biological hazards due to employee handling, and food allergen hazards. Sanitation controls must include, as appropriate to the facility and the food, procedures, practices, and processes for the:
(c)(3)(i) (i) Cleanliness of food-contact surfaces, including food-contact surfaces of utensils and equipment;
(c)(3)(ii) (ii) Prevention of allergen cross-contact and cross-contamination from insanitary objects and from personnel to food, food packaging material, and other food-contact surfaces and from raw product to processed product.
(c)(4) (4) Supply-chain controls. Supply-chain controls include the supply-chain program as required by subpart G of this part.
(c)(5) (5) Recall plan. Recall plan as required by § 117.139.
(c)(6) (6) Other controls. Preventive controls include any other procedures, practices, and processes necessary to satisfy the requirements of paragraph (a) of this section. Examples of other controls include hygiene training and other current good manufacturing practices.
ideal_answer:
All three are kinds of preventive control under 21 CFR 117.135(c), which lists them as, among others, process controls, food allergen controls and sanitation controls. They share the same frame: you must identify and implement preventive controls to provide assurances that any hazards requiring a preventive control will be significantly minimized or prevented and that the food will not be adulterated under section 402 of the Act (117.135(a)(1)); they include controls at critical control points, if there are any, and controls other than at CCPs that are also appropriate for food safety (117.135(a)(2)); and they must be written (117.135(b)). What differs is what each controls.

Process controls (117.135(c)(1)) are procedures, practices and processes to ensure the control of parameters during operations such as heat processing, acidifying, irradiating and refrigerating foods. They must include, as appropriate to the nature of the control and its role in the facility's food safety system, the parameters associated with control of the hazard, and the maximum or minimum value, or combination of values, to which any biological, chemical or physical parameter must be controlled to significantly minimize or prevent a hazard requiring a process control. So a process control is characterised by measurable parameters and limits.

Food allergen controls (117.135(c)(2)) are procedures, practices and processes to control food allergens, and must include those employed for ensuring protection of food from allergen cross-contact, including during storage, handling and use, and for labeling the finished food, including ensuring the finished food is not misbranded under section 403(w) of the Act. So an allergen control has two limbs - physical separation and correct labeling.

Sanitation controls (117.135(c)(3)) are procedures, practices and processes to ensure that the facility is maintained in a sanitary condition adequate to significantly minimize or prevent hazards such as environmental pathogens, biological hazards due to employee handling and food allergen hazards, and must include those for the cleanliness of food-contact surfaces, including those of utensils and equipment, and for prevention of allergen cross-contact and cross-contamination from insanitary objects and from personnel to food, packaging material and other food-contact surfaces, and from raw product to processed product.

Note the overlap, which the regulation itself creates: allergen cross-contact is addressed by both the allergen controls in (c)(2)(i) and the sanitation controls in (c)(3)(ii). The other categories in the same list are supply-chain controls, which comprise the supply-chain program required by subpart G (117.135(c)(4)); the recall plan required by 117.139 (117.135(c)(5)); and other controls, being any other procedures necessary to satisfy 117.135(a), with hygiene training and other CGMPs as examples (117.135(c)(6)).

question: What corrections and removals are exempt from reporting under Part 806 but still require records?
evidence:
[21 CFR 806.10] Reports of corrections and removals.
(a) (a) Each device manufacturer or importer shall submit a written report to FDA of any correction or removal of a device initiated by such manufacturer or importer if the correction or removal was initiated:
(a)(1) (1) To reduce a risk to health posed by the device; or
(a)(2) (2) To remedy a violation of the act caused by the device which may present a risk to health unless the information has already been provided as set forth in paragraph (f) of this section or the corrective or removal action is exempt from the reporting requirements under § 806.1(b).
(b) (b) The manufacturer or importer shall submit any report required by paragraph (a) of this section within 10-working days of initiating such correction or removal.
(c) (c) The manufacturer or importer shall include the following information in the report:
(c)(1) (1) The seven digit registration number of the entity responsible for submission of the report of corrective or removal action (if applicable), the month, day, and year that the report is made, and a sequence number (i.e., 001 for the first report, 002 for the second report, 003 etc.), and the report type designation “C” or “R”. For example, the complete number for the first correction report submitted on June 1, 1997, will appear as follows for a firm with the registration number 1234567: 1234567-6/1/97-001-C. The second correction report number submitted by the same firm on July 1, 1997, would be 1234567-7/1/97-002-C etc. For removals, the number will appear as follows: 1234567-6/1/97-001-R and 1234567-7/1/97-002-R, etc. Firms that do not have a seven digit registration number may use seven zeros followed by the month, date, year, and sequence number (i.e. 0000000-6/1/97-001-C for corrections and 0000000-7/1/97-001-R for removals). Reports received without a seven digit registration number will be assigned a seven digit central file number by the district office reviewing the reports.
(c)(2) (2) The name, address, and telephone number of the manufacturer or importer, and the name, title, address, and telephone number of the manufacturer or importer representative responsible for conducting the device correction or removal.
(c)(3) (3) The brand name and the common name, classification name, or usual name of the device and the intended use of the device.
(c)(4) (4) Marketing status of the device, i.e., any applicable premarket notification number, premarket approval number, or indication that the device is a preamendments device, and the device listing number. A manufacturer or importer that does not have an FDA establishment registration number shall indicate in the report whether it has ever registered with FDA.
(c)(5) (5) The unique device identifier (UDI) that appears on the device label or on the device package, or the device identifier, universal product code (UPC), model, catalog, or code number of the device and the manufacturing lot or serial number of the device or other identification number.
(c)(6) (6) The manufacturer's name, address, telephone number, and contact person if different from that of the person submitting the report.
(c)(7) (7) A description of the event(s) giving rise to the information reported and the corrective or removal actions that have been, and are expected to be taken.
(c)(8) (8) Any illness or injuries that have occurred with use of the device. If applicable, include the medical device report numbers.
(c)(9) (9) The total number of devices manufactured or distributed subject to the correction or removal and the number in the same batch, lot, or equivalent unit of production subject to the correction or removal.
(c)(10) (10) The date of manufacture or distribution and the device's expiration date or expected life.
(c)(11) (11) The names, addresses, and telephone numbers of all domestic and foreign consignees of the device and the dates and number of devices distributed to each such consignee.
(c)(12) (12) A copy of all communications regarding the correction or removal and the names and addresses of all recipients of the communications not provided in accordance with paragraph (c)(11) of this section.
(c)(13) (13) If any required information is not immediately available, a statement as to why it is not available and when it will be submitted.
(d) (d) If, after submitting a report under this part, a manufacturer or importer determines that the same correction or removal should be extended to additional lots or batches of the same device, the manufacturer or importer shall within 10-working days of initiating the extension of the correction or removal, amend the report by submitting an amendment citing the original report number assigned according to paragraph (c)(1) of this section, all of the information required by paragraph (c)(2), and any information required by paragraphs (c)(3) through (c)(12) of this section that is different from the information submitted in the original report. The manufacturer or importer shall also provide a statement in accordance with paragraph (c)(13) of this section for any required information that is not readily available.
(e) (e) A report submitted by a manufacturer or importer under this section (and any release by FDA of that report or information) does not necessarily reflect a conclusion by the manufacturer, importer, or FDA that the report or information constitutes an admission that the device caused or contributed to a death or serious injury. A manufacturer or importer need not admit, and may deny, that the report or information submitted under this section constitutes an admission that the device caused or contributed to a death or serious injury.
(f) (f) No report of correction or removal is required under this part, if a report of the correction or removal is required and has been submitted under parts 803 or 1004 of this chapter.

[21 CFR 806.20] Records of corrections and removals not required to be reported.
(a) (a) Each device manufacturer or importer who initiates a correction or removal of a device that is not required to be reported to FDA under § 806.10 shall keep a record of such correction or removal.
(b) (b) Records of corrections and removals not required to be reported to FDA under § 806.10 shall contain the following information:
(b)(1) (1) The brand name, common or usual name, classification, name and product code if known, and the intended use of the device.
(b)(2) (2) The unique device identifier (UDI) of the device, or the device identifier, universal product code (UPC), model, catalog, or code number of the device and the manufacturing lot or serial number of the device or other identification number.
(b)(3) (3) A description of the event(s) giving rise to the information reported and the corrective or removal action that has been, and is expected to be taken.
(b)(4) (4) Justification for not reporting the correction or removal action to FDA, which shall contain conclusions and any followups, and be reviewed and evaluated by a designated person.
(b)(5) (5) A copy of all communications regarding the correction or removal.
(c) (c) The manufacturer or importer shall retain records required under this section for a period of 2 years beyond the expected life of the device, even if the manufacturer or importer has ceased to manufacture or import the device. Records required to be maintained under paragraph (b) of this section must be transferred to the new manufacturer or importer of the device and maintained for the required period of time.

[21 CFR 806.1] Scope.
(a) (a) This part implements the provisions of section 519(g) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act (the act) requiring device manufacturers and importers to report promptly to the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) certain actions concerning device corrections and removals, and to maintain records of all corrections and removals regardless of whether such corrections and removals are required to be reported to FDA.
(b) (b) The following actions are exempt from the reporting requirements of this part:
(b)(1) (1) Actions taken by device manufacturers or importers to improve the performance or quality of a device but that do not reduce a risk to health posed by the device or remedy a violation of the act caused by the device.
(b)(2) (2) Market withdrawal as defined in § 806.2(i)
(b)(3) (3) Routine servicing as defined in § 806.2(l).
(b)(4) (4) Stock recovery as defined in § 806.2(m).

(a) (a) Under this subpart, for single entity or co-packaged combination products, compliance with all applicable current good manufacturing practice requirements for the combination product shall be achieved through the design and implementation of a current good manufacturing practice operating system that is demonstrated to comply with:
(a)(1) (1) The specifics of each set of current good manufacturing practice regulations listed under § 4.3 as they apply to each constituent part included in the combination product; or
(a)(2) (2) Paragraph (b) of this section.
(b) (b) If you elect to establish a current good manufacturing practice operating system in accordance with paragraph (b) of this section, the following requirements apply:
(b)(1) (1) If the combination product includes a device constituent part and a drug constituent part, and the current good manufacturing practice operating system has been shown to comply with the drug CGMP requirements or the medical gas CGMP requirements, as applicable, the following clauses of ISO 13485 (together with the definitions in Clause 3 of ISO 9000), which is incorporated by reference into the QMSR under § 820.7 of this chapter, and certain other provisions within the QMSR must also be shown to have been satisfied; upon demonstration that these requirements have been satisfied, no additional showing of compliance with respect to the QMSR need be made:
(b)(1)(i) (i) General requirements and management responsibility. Clause 4.1, Clause 5 and its subclauses, Clause 6.1 of ISO 13485, and § 820.10 of this chapter;
(b)(1)(ii) (ii) Design and development. Clause 7.3 and its subclauses of ISO 13485. The organization shall document one or more processes for risk management in product realization. Records of risk management activities shall be maintained;
(b)(1)(iii) (iii) Purchasing. Clause 7.4. and its subclauses of ISO 13485;
(b)(1)(iv) (iv) Analysis of data, improvement, and complaint handling. Clause 8.2.2 and § 820.35(a) of this chapter, Clause 8.4, and Clause 8.5. and its subclauses of ISO 13485;
(b)(1)(v) (v) Installation activities. Clause 7.5.3 of ISO 13485; and
