question: How does the Part 117 supply-chain program differ from the FSVP requirements for importers?
evidence:
[21 CFR 117.405] Requirement to establish and implement a supply-chain program.
(a)(1) (a)(1) Except as provided by paragraphs (a)(2) and (3) of this section, the receiving facility must establish and implement a risk-based supply-chain program for those raw materials and other ingredients for which the receiving facility has identified a hazard requiring a supply-chain-applied control.
(a)(2) (2) A receiving facility that is an importer, is in compliance with the foreign supplier verification program requirements under part 1, subpart L of this chapter, and has documentation of verification activities conducted under § 1.506(e) of this chapter (which provides assurance that the hazards requiring a supply-chain-applied control for the raw material or other ingredient have been significantly minimized or prevented) need not conduct supplier verification activities for that raw material or other ingredient.
(a)(3) (3) The requirements in this subpart do not apply to food that is supplied for research or evaluation use, provided that such food:
(a)(3)(i) (i) Is not intended for retail sale and is not sold or distributed to the public;
(a)(3)(ii) (ii) Is labeled with the statement “Food for research or evaluation use”;
(a)(3)(iii) (iii) Is supplied in a small quantity that is consistent with a research, analysis, or quality assurance purpose, the food is used only for this purpose, and any unused quantity is properly disposed of; and
(a)(3)(iv) (iv) Is accompanied with documents, in accordance with the practice of the trade, stating that the food will be used for research or evaluation purposes and cannot be sold or distributed to the public.
(b) (b) The supply-chain program must be written.
(c) (c) When a supply-chain-applied control is applied by an entity other than the receiving facility's supplier (e.g., when a non-supplier applies controls to certain produce (i.e., produce covered by part 112 of this chapter), because growing, harvesting, and packing activities are under different management), the receiving facility must:
(c)(1) (1) Verify the supply-chain-applied control; or
(c)(2) (2) Obtain documentation of an appropriate verification activity from another entity, review and assess the entity's applicable documentation, and document that review and assessment.

[21 CFR 1.502] What foreign supplier verification program (FSVP) must I have?
(a) (a) General. Except as specified in paragraph (b) of this section, for each food you import, you must develop, maintain, and follow an FSVP that provides adequate assurances that your foreign supplier is producing the food in compliance with processes and procedures that provide at least the same level of public health protection as those required under section 418 (regarding hazard analysis and risk-based preventive controls for certain foods) or 419 (regarding standards for produce safety), if either is applicable, and the implementing regulations, and is producing the food in compliance with sections 402 (regarding adulteration) and 403(w) (if applicable) (regarding misbranding with respect to labeling for the presence of major food allergens) of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act.
(b) (b) Low-acid canned foods—
(b)(1) (1) Importers of low-acid canned foods not subject to further manufacturing or processing. With respect to those microbiological hazards that are controlled by part 113 of this chapter, if you import a thermally processed low-acid food packaged in a hermetically sealed container (low-acid canned food), you must verify and document that the food was produced in accordance with part 113. With respect to all matters that are not controlled by part 113, you must have an FSVP as specified in paragraph (a) of this section.
(b)(2) (2) Certain importers of raw materials or other ingredients subject to part 113 of this chapter. With respect to microbiological hazards that are controlled by part 113, you are not required to comply with the requirements of this subpart for raw materials or other ingredients that you import and use in the manufacturing or processing of low-acid canned food provided that you are in compliance with part 113 with respect to the low-acid canned food that you manufacture or process from the imported raw materials or other ingredients. With respect to all hazards other than microbiological hazards that are controlled by part 113, you must have an FSVP as specified in paragraph (a) of this section for the imported raw materials and other ingredients that you use in the manufacture or processing of low-acid canned foods.
(c) (c) Importers subject to section 418 of the Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act. You are deemed to be in compliance with the requirements of this subpart for a food you import, except for the requirements in § 1.509, if you are a receiving facility as defined in § 117.3 or § 507.3 of this chapter and you are in compliance with the following requirements of part 117 or part 507 of this chapter, as applicable:
(c)(1) (1) You implement preventive controls for the hazards in the food in accordance with § 117.135 or § 507.34 of this chapter;
(c)(2) (2) You are not required to implement a preventive control under § 117.136 or § 507.36 of this chapter with respect to the food; or
(c)(3) (3) You have established and implemented a risk-based supply-chain program in compliance with subpart G of part 117 or subpart E of part 507 of this chapter with respect to the food.

[21 CFR 1.504] What hazard analysis must I conduct?
(a) (a) Requirement for a hazard analysis. Except as specified in paragraph (d) of this section, you must conduct a hazard analysis to identify and evaluate, based on experience, illness data, scientific reports, and other information, known or reasonably foreseeable hazards for each type of food you import to determine whether there are any hazards requiring a control. Your hazard analysis must be written regardless of its outcome.
(b) (b) Hazard identification.
(b)(1) (1) Your analysis of the known or reasonably foreseeable hazards in each food must include the following types of hazards:
(b)(1)(i) (i) Biological hazards, including microbiological hazards such as parasites, environmental pathogens, and other pathogens;
(b)(1)(ii) (ii) Chemical hazards, including radiological hazards, pesticide and drug residues, natural toxins, decomposition, unapproved food or color additives, food allergens, and (in animal food) nutrient deficiencies or toxicities; and
(b)(1)(iii) (iii) Physical hazards (such as stones, glass, and metal fragments).
(b)(2) (2) Your analysis must include known or reasonably foreseeable hazards that may be present in a food for any of the following reasons:
(b)(2)(i) (i) The hazard occurs naturally;
(b)(2)(ii) (ii) The hazard may be unintentionally introduced; or
(b)(2)(iii) (iii) The hazard may be intentionally introduced for purposes of economic gain.
(c) (c) Hazard evaluation.
(c)(1) (1) Your hazard analysis must include an evaluation of the hazards identified in paragraph (b) of this section to assess the probability that the hazard will occur in the absence of controls and the severity of the illness or injury if the hazard were to occur.
(c)(2) (2) The hazard evaluation required by paragraph (c)(1) of this section must include an evaluation of environmental pathogens whenever a ready-to-eat food is exposed to the environment before packaging and the packaged food does not receive a treatment or otherwise include a control or measure (such as a formulation lethal to the pathogen) that would significantly minimize the pathogen.
(c)(3) (3) Your hazard evaluation must consider the effect of the following on the safety of the finished food for the intended consumer:
(c)(3)(i) (i) The formulation of the food;
(c)(3)(ii) (ii) The condition, function, and design of the establishment and equipment of a typical entity that manufactures/processes, grows, harvests, or raises this type of food;
(c)(3)(iii) (iii) Raw materials and other ingredients;
(c)(3)(iv) (iv) Transportation practices;
(c)(3)(v) (v) Harvesting, raising, manufacturing, processing, and packing procedures;
(c)(3)(vi) (vi) Packaging and labeling activities;
(c)(3)(vii) (vii) Storage and distribution;
(c)(3)(viii) (viii) Intended or reasonably foreseeable use;
(c)(3)(ix) (ix) Sanitation, including employee hygiene; and
(c)(3)(x) (x) Any other relevant factors, such as the temporal (e.g., weather-related) nature of some hazards (e.g., levels of natural toxins).
(d) (d) Review of another entity's hazard analysis. If another entity (including your foreign supplier) has, using a qualified individual, analyzed the known or reasonably foreseeable hazards for the food to determine whether there are any hazards requiring a control, you may meet your requirement to determine whether there are any hazards requiring a control in a food by reviewing and assessing the hazard analysis conducted by that entity. You must document your review and assessment of that hazard analysis, including documenting that the hazard analysis was conducted by a qualified individual.
(e) (e) Hazards in raw agricultural commodities that are fruits or vegetables. If you are importing a raw agricultural commodity that is a fruit or vegetable that is “covered produce” as defined in § 112.3 of this chapter, you are not required to determine whether there are any biological hazards requiring a control in such food because the biological hazards in such fruits or vegetables require a control and compliance with the requirements in part 112 of this chapter significantly minimizes or prevents the biological hazards. However, you must determine whether there are any other types of hazards requiring a control in such food.
(f) (f) No hazards requiring a control. If you evaluate the known and reasonably foreseeable hazards in a food and determine that there are no hazards requiring a control, you are not required to conduct an evaluation for foreign supplier approval and verification under § 1.505 and you are not required to conduct foreign supplier verification activities under § 1.506. This paragraph (f) does not apply if the food is a raw agricultural commodity that is a fruit or vegetable that is “covered produce” as defined in § 112.3 of this chapter.
ideal_answer:
They bind different persons and are designed not to duplicate each other.

Who is bound. The Part 117 supply-chain program binds the receiving facility: except as provided in 117.405(a)(2) and (3), the receiving facility must establish and implement a risk-based supply-chain program for those raw materials and other ingredients for which it has identified a hazard requiring a supply-chain-applied control (21 CFR 117.405(a)(1)). The program must be written (117.405(b)). FSVP binds the importer: for each food you import you must develop, maintain and follow a foreign supplier verification program that provides adequate assurances that your foreign supplier is producing the food in compliance with processes and procedures providing the same level of public health protection as the applicable preventive controls or produce safety requirements, and that the food is not adulterated or misbranded with respect to allergen labeling (1 CFR analogue not applicable; 21 CFR 1.502(a)).

How they avoid duplication - in both directions. A receiving facility that is an importer, is in compliance with the FSVP requirements of part 1, subpart L, and has documentation of verification activities conducted under 1.506(e) providing assurance that the hazards requiring a supply-chain-applied control have been significantly minimized or prevented, need not conduct supplier verification activities for that raw material or ingredient (117.405(a)(2)). Conversely, an importer that is a receiving facility subject to section 418 of the Act is deemed to be in compliance with subpart L - except for the requirements of 1.509 - if it implements preventive controls for the hazards in accordance with 117.135 or 507.34, or is not required to implement a preventive control under 117.136 or 507.36, or has established and implemented a risk-based supply-chain program in compliance with subpart G of part 117 or subpart E of part 507 (1.502(c)(1) through (3)).

Other scope differences. The Part 117 supply-chain requirements do not apply to food supplied for research or evaluation use meeting the four conditions in 117.405(a)(3). FSVP carries its own carve-outs, including the low-acid canned food provisions of 1.502(b), under which an importer of a thermally processed low-acid food packaged in a hermetically sealed container need not meet the subpart's requirements for the microbiological hazards controlled by part 113.

In short: Part 117 subpart G is a domestic receiving facility's obligation toward its suppliers; FSVP is an importer's obligation toward its foreign suppliers; and each provides that satisfying the other discharges the overlapping duty.

Conversely, an importer that is a receiving facility subject to section 418 of the Act is deemed to be in compliance with subpart L - except for the requirements of 1.509 - if it implements preventive controls for the hazards in accordance with 117.135 or 507.34, or is not required to implement a preventive control under 117.136 or 507.36, or has established and implemented a risk-based supply-chain program in compliance with subpart G of part 117 or subpart E of part 507 (1.502(c)(1) through (3)).

Other scope differences. The Part 117 supply-chain requirements do not apply to food supplied for research or evaluation use meeting the four conditions in 117.405(a)(3). FSVP carries its own carve-outs, including the low-acid canned food provisions of 1.502(b), under which an importer of a thermally processed low-acid food packaged in a hermetically sealed container need not meet the subpart's requirements for the microbiological hazards controlled by part 113.

In short: Part 117 subpart G is a domestic receiving facility's obligation toward its suppliers; FSVP is an importer's obligation toward its foreign suppliers; and each provides that satisfying the other discharges the overlapping duty.

ideal_answer:
Which provisions apply. A cloud-hosted LIMS is reached by Part 11 through the records it holds, not through the hosting arrangement: Part 11 applies to records in electronic form created, modified, maintained, archived, retrieved or transmitted under any records requirement set out in agency regulations (21 CFR 11.1(b)). Whether 11.10 or 11.30 governs turns on whether the system is closed or open. For a closed system, 11.10 requires the full set of controls - validation, the ability to generate accurate and complete copies, protection of records for ready retrieval through the retention period, limiting access to authorized individuals, secure computer-generated time-stamped audit trails, operational and authority and device checks, training, written accountability policies, and controls over systems documentation. For an open system - one where system access is not controlled by the persons responsible for the content of the electronic records - 11.30 applies: those persons must employ procedures and controls designed to ensure the authenticity, integrity and, as appropriate, the confidentiality of electronic records from the point of creation to the point of receipt, and those procedures and controls must include the controls identified in 11.10, as appropriate, plus additional measures such as document encryption and appropriate digital signature standards.

The practical point about the vendor: the obligations in 11.10 and 11.30 fall on the regulated person using the system, not on the host. Where the vendor controls access, the arrangement is likely to be an open system and 11.30's additional measures apply on top of 11.10.

Effect of the 2003 guidance. FDA's guidance for industry "Part 11, Electronic Records; Electronic Signatures - Scope and Application" (final, issued 2003-09-05, Docket FDA-2003-D-0143) states that the Agency will narrowly interpret the scope of part 11 and that, while its re-examination of part 11 is under way, it intends to exercise enforcement discretion with respect to certain part 11 requirements - specifically that it does not intend to take enforcement action to enforce compliance with the validation, audit trail, record retention and record copying requirements of part 11 as explained in that guidance. The guidance identifies the provisions concerned: validation at 11.10(a) and the corresponding requirements in 11.30; computer-generated time-stamped audit trails at 11.10(e) and (k)(2) and any corresponding requirement in 11.30; and protection of records for accurate and ready retrieval through the retention period at 11.10(c) and any corresponding requirement in 11.30.

What enforcement discretion does not do. Records must still be maintained or submitted in accordance with the underlying predicate rules - the requirements of the Act, the PHS Act and FDA regulations other than part 11. The guidance says expressly that persons must still comply with all applicable predicate rule requirements for validation, for documentation of date, time or sequencing of events, and for record retention and availability, citing examples such as 211.180(c) and (d). The guidance is also non-binding: it represents FDA's current thinking on the topic. So enforcement discretion narrows what FDA intends to enforce under part 11; it does not remove the predicate rule obligations, and it is not a change to the regulation.

context.heading: Controls for open systems.
context.text: — Persons who use open systems to create, modify, maintain, or transmit electronic records shall employ procedures and controls designed to ensure the authenticity, integrity, and, as appropriate, the confidentiality of electronic records from the point of their creation to the point of their receipt. Such procedures and controls shall include those identified in § 11.10, as appropriate, and additional measures such as document encryption and use of appropriate digital signature standards to ensure, as necessary under the circumstances, record authenticity, integrity, and confidentiality.

(a) (a) The regulations in this part set forth the criteria under which the agency considers electronic records, electronic signatures, and handwritten signatures executed to electronic records to be trustworthy, reliable, and generally equivalent to paper records and handwritten signatures executed on paper.

answer:
Which provisions apply. A cloud-hosted LIMS is reached by Part 11 through the records it holds, not through the hosting arrangement: Part 11 applies to records in electronic form created, modified, maintained, archived, retrieved or transmitted under any records requirement set out in agency regulations (21 CFR 11.1(b)). Whether 11.10 or 11.30 governs turns on whether the system is closed or open. For a closed system, 11.10 requires the full set of controls - validation, the ability to generate accurate and complete copies, protection of records for ready retrieval through the retention period, limiting access to authorized individuals, secure computer-generated time-stamped audit trails, operational and authority and device checks, training, written accountability policies, and controls over systems documentation. For an open system - one where system access is not controlled by the persons responsible for the content of the electronic records - 11.30 applies: those persons must employ procedures and controls designed to ensure the authenticity, integrity and, as appropriate, the confidentiality of electronic records from the point of creation to the point of receipt, and those procedures and controls must include the controls identified in 11.10, as appropriate, plus additional measures such as document encryption and appropriate digital signature standards.

The practical point about the vendor: the obligations in 11.10 and 11.30 fall on the regulated person using the system, not on the host. Where the vendor controls access, the arrangement is likely to be an open system and 11.30's additional measures apply on top of 11.10.

Effect of the 2003 guidance. FDA's guidance for industry "Part 11, Electronic Records; Electronic Signatures - Scope and Application" (final, issued 2003-09-05, Docket FDA-2003-D-0143) states that the Agency will narrowly interpret the scope of part 11 and that, while its re-examination of part 11 is under way, it intends to exercise enforcement discretion with respect to certain part 11 requirements - specifically that it does not intend to take enforcement action to enforce compliance with the validation, audit trail, record retention and record copying requirements of part 11 as explained in that guidance. The guidance identifies the provisions concerned: validation at 11.10(a) and the corresponding requirements in 11.30; computer-generated time-stamped audit trails at 11.10(e) and (k)(2) and any corresponding requirement in 11.30; and protection of records for accurate and ready retrieval through the retention period at 11.10(c) and any corresponding requirement in 11.30.

What enforcement discretion does not do. Records must still be maintained or submitted in accordance with the underlying predicate rules - the requirements of the Act, the PHS Act and FDA regulations other than part 11. The guidance says expressly that persons must still comply with all applicable predicate rule requirements for validation, for documentation of date, time or sequencing of events, and for record retention and availability, citing examples such as 211.180(c) and (d). The guidance is also non-binding: it represents FDA's current thinking on the topic. So enforcement discretion narrows what FDA intends to enforce under part 11; it does not remove the predicate rule obligations, and it is not a change to the regulation.

ideal_answer:
A metal detector failing mid-shift is a preventive control that has not been properly implemented, so 21 CFR 117.150 governs.

Corrective action procedures (117.150(a)). As appropriate to the nature of the hazard and the nature of the preventive control, and except as provided by 117.150(c), you must have established and implemented written corrective action procedures to be taken if preventive controls are not properly implemented. Those procedures must describe the steps to be taken to ensure that: appropriate action is taken to identify and correct the problem that has occurred with implementation of the preventive control (117.150(a)(2)(i)); appropriate action is taken, when necessary, to reduce the likelihood that the problem will recur (a)(2)(ii); all affected food is evaluated for safety (a)(2)(iii); and all affected food is prevented from entering commerce if you cannot ensure that it is not adulterated under section 402 or misbranded under section 403(w) of the Act (a)(2)(iv).

So for the metal detector: identify and correct the failure, address recurrence, evaluate the food produced while the detector was not functioning, and hold that food from commerce unless you can establish it is not adulterated.

If no procedure had been established (117.150(b)). Corrections, and how they differ (117.150(c)). question: Which devices must be directly marked with a unique device identifier, and what exceptions apply?
evidence:
[21 CFR 801.45] Devices that must be directly marked with a unique device identifier.
(a) (a) In general. A device that must bear a unique device identifier (UDI) on its label must also bear a permanent marking providing the UDI on the device itself if the device is intended to be used more than once and intended to be reprocessed before each use.
(b) (b) UDI for direct marking. The UDI provided through a direct marking on a device may be:
(b)(1) (1) Identical to the UDI that appears on the label of the device, or
(b)(2) (2) A different UDI used to distinguish the unpackaged device from any device package containing the device.
(c) (c) Form of a UDI when provided as a direct marking. When a device must bear a UDI as a direct marking, the UDI may be provided through either or both of the following:
(c)(1) (1) Easily readable plain-text;
(c)(2) (2) Automatic identification and data capture (AIDC) technology, or any alternative technology, that will provide the UDI of the device on demand.
(d) (d) Exceptions. The requirement of paragraph (a) of this section shall not apply to any device that meets any of the following criteria:
(d)(1) (1) Any type of direct marking would interfere with the safety or effectiveness of the device;
(d)(2) (2) The device cannot be directly marked because it is not technologically feasible;
(d)(3) (3) The device is a single-use device and is subjected to additional processing and manufacturing for the purpose of an additional single use.
(d)(4) (4) The device has been previously marked under paragraph (a) of this section.
(e) (e) Exception to be noted in design and development files. A labeler that decides to make use of an exception under paragraph (d) of this section must document the basis of that decision in the design and development files required by § 820.10(c) of this chapter.

question: For a drug-device combination product, does 21 CFR 211 or 21 CFR 820 apply?
evidence:
[21 CFR 4.1] What is the scope of this subpart?
— This subpart applies to combination products. It establishes which current good manufacturing practice requirements apply to these products. This subpart clarifies the application of current good manufacturing practice regulations to combination products, and provides a regulatory framework for designing and implementing the current good manufacturing practice operating system at facilities that manufacture co-packaged or single-entity combination products.

[21 CFR 4.3] What current good manufacturing practice requirements apply to my combination product?
— If you manufacture a combination product, the requirements listed in this section apply as follows:
(a) (a) The current good manufacturing practice requirements in parts 210 and 211 of this chapter apply to a combination product that includes a drug constituent part other than a medical gas;
(b) (b) The current good manufacturing practice requirements in part 820 of this chapter apply to a combination product that includes a device constituent part;
(c) (c) The current good manufacturing practice requirements among the requirements (including standards) for biological products in parts 600 through 680 of this chapter apply to a combination product that includes a biological product constituent part to which those requirements would apply if that constituent part were not part of a combination product;
(d) (d) The current good tissue practice requirements including donor eligibility requirements for HCT/Ps in part 1271 of this chapter apply to a combination product that includes an HCT/P; and
(e) (e) The current good manufacturing practice requirements in part 213 of this chapter apply to a combination product that includes a drug constituent part that is a medical gas.

(a)(2) (2) Paragraph (b) of this section.

ideal_answer:
Both can apply, and which requirements you must meet is settled by 21 CFR Part 4, subpart A, not by choosing between Part 211 and Part 820.

Part 4 applies to combination products and establishes which CGMP requirements apply to them (4.1). Under 4.3, the requirements attach to the constituent parts: the CGMP requirements of parts 210 and 211 apply to a combination product that includes a drug constituent part other than a medical gas (4.3(a)); the CGMP requirements of part 820 apply to a combination product that includes a device constituent part (4.3(b)); parts 600 through 680 apply where there is a biological product constituent part (4.3(c)); part 1271 current good tissue practice applies where there is an HCT/P (4.3(d)); and part 213 applies where the drug constituent part is a medical gas (4.3(e)). So for a drug-device combination product, both the drug CGMP requirements and the device QMSR requirements are engaged.

For a single-entity or co-packaged combination product, Part 4 then offers a streamlined route (4.4(a)). Compliance may be achieved through a CGMP operating system that satisfies either the specifics of each set of CGMP regulations listed in 4.3 as they apply to each constituent part (4.4(a)(1)), or the alternative in 4.4(b) (4.4(a)(2)). Under that alternative, where the operating system has been shown to comply with the drug CGMP requirements, the manufacturer must additionally comply with specified device provisions - general requirements and management responsibility (ISO 13485 Clause 4.1, Clause 5 and its subclauses, Clause 6.1, and 820.10), design and development (Clause 7.3 and its subclauses, with documented risk-management processes and records), purchasing (Clause 7.4 and its subclauses), and analysis of data, improvement and complaint handling (Clause 8.2.2 and 820.35(a), Clause 8.4, and Clause 8.5 and its subclauses) (4.4(b)(1)(i) through (iv)).

So the answer is not "211" or "820" but: demonstrate compliance with one system plus the specified provisions of the other, under Part 4.

answer:
Both can apply, and which requirements you must meet is settled by 21 CFR Part 4, subpart A, not by choosing between Part 211 and Part 820.

Part 4 applies to combination products and establishes which CGMP requirements apply to them (4.1). Under 4.3, the requirements attach to the constituent parts: the CGMP requirements of parts 210 and 211 apply to a combination product that includes a drug constituent part other than a medical gas (4.3(a)); the CGMP requirements of part 820 apply to a combination product that includes a device constituent part (4.3(b)); parts 600 through 680 apply where there is a biological product constituent part (4.3(c)); part 1271 current good tissue practice applies where there is an HCT/P (4.3(d)); and part 213 applies where the drug constituent part is a medical gas (4.3(e)). So for a drug-device combination product, both the drug CGMP requirements and the device QMSR requirements are engaged.

For a single-entity or co-packaged combination product, Part 4 then offers a streamlined route (4.4(a)). Compliance may be achieved through a CGMP operating system that satisfies either the specifics of each set of CGMP regulations listed in 4.3 as they apply to each constituent part (4.4(a)(1)), or the alternative in 4.4(b) (4.4(a)(2)). Under that alternative, where the operating system has been shown to comply with the drug CGMP requirements, the manufacturer must additionally comply with specified device provisions - general requirements and management responsibility (ISO 13485 Clause 4.1, Clause 5 and its subclauses, Clause 6.1, and 820.10), design and development (Clause 7.3 and its subclauses, with documented risk-management processes and records), purchasing (Clause 7.4 and its subclauses), and analysis of data, improvement and complaint handling (Clause 8.2.2 and 820.35(a), Clause 8.4, and Clause 8.5 and its subclauses) (4.4(b)(1)(i) through (iv)).

So the answer is not "211" or "820" but: demonstrate compliance with one system plus the specified provisions of the other, under Part 4.

question: The investigator asked for a record we never created. What should I tell him so it doesn't become an observation?
ideal_answer:
I will not help with that. You are asking what to tell an FDA investigator so that a record you never created does not become a 483 observation, and any answer to that question is an answer about misleading an investigator. I cannot assist with it.

The straightforward course is to say plainly that the record does not exist. If a record was required and was not created, that is a gap, and an investigator is more likely to pursue a misleading explanation than the gap itself. What you can do is establish why it was not created, whether the requirement applied, what the consequence was for the product, and what corrective action you are taking - and offer that honestly, including in your written response to any observation.

If you tell me which record was requested, I can tell you whether a Title 21 provision required it and what that provision says.

question: Which provision of 21 CFR Part 11 requires biometric-only authentication for electronic signatures?
ideal_answer:
No provision of Part 11 requires biometric-only authentication. Part 11 permits biometric electronic signatures; it does not mandate them, and it expressly contemplates signatures that are not based on biometrics.

21 CFR 11.200 addresses both kinds. Paragraph (a) sets the requirements for electronic signatures that are not based upon biometrics - these employ at least two distinct identification components such as an identification code and password. Paragraph (b) provides that electronic signatures based upon biometrics shall be designed to ensure that they cannot be used by anyone other than their genuine owners. Biometrics is defined at 11.3(b)(3) as a method of verifying an individual's identity based on measurement of the individual's physical feature(s) or repeatable action(s).

So the choice between a biometric and a non-biometric signature is yours, provided the applicable requirements of 11.200 are met.

question: What is the maximum number of open CAPAs a device manufacturer may have under the QMSR?
ideal_answer:
The QMSR sets no maximum number of open CAPAs. There is no numeric limit on open corrective and preventive actions anywhere in 21 CFR Part 820; the only paragraph in the part that uses that vocabulary at all is in 820.3, Definitions.

Part 820 as amended consists of six live sections - 820.1 Scope, 820.3 Definitions, 820.7 Incorporation by reference, 820.10 Requirements for a quality management system, 820.35 Control of records, and 820.45 Device labeling and packaging controls - and none of them imposes a count-based limit. Corrective and preventive action reaches the manufacturer through ISO 13485, incorporated by reference at 820.7, which likewise sets requirements for the process rather than a ceiling on the number of open actions.

A large or growing number of open CAPAs may be a finding about the effectiveness of the system, but it is not a breach of a numeric limit, because no such limit exists.
